337.title: The second truth
337.hook: craving for sense pleasure, for being, for not-being (SN 56.11)
337.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers explain the second truth through the three kinds of craving, and meditators in many schools learn to notice wanting and not-wanting as they arise, without acting on them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pariññeyya, the first truth's task, to be known all the way around. Your line: understand it. Now, the cause.

Thirst is a strange feeling when you really look at it. It isn't in your stomach, like hunger. It's a dryness that pulls. It narrows the world: a desert traveler doesn't notice the sunset, only the water he hasn't got. And the moment it's quenched, it starts quietly building again. When the Buddha named the cause of dukkha in the first sermon, he didn't pick fate, or bad luck, or the stars. He picked thirst.
screen: `NOT HUNGER: A DRYNESS THAT PULLS.` → `THE WORLD NARROWS.` → `HE PICKED THIRST.`

segments.voice: The second truth is samudaya, the arising, where dukkha comes from. In the first sermon the Buddha says it's taṇhā, a Pali word whose plain meaning is thirst; English translations often say craving. He describes it as the thirst that leads to becoming again, bound up with delight and lust, finding its pleasure now here, now there. Then he names three thirsts. The first is thirst for sense pleasure: the next taste, the next song, the next scroll. The second is thirst for being: to exist, to become someone, to have your name last. The third is the surprising one, thirst for not-being: to make something disappear, to not be here, to have this whole feeling just stop. It sounds like the opposite of craving, but the sutta counts it as craving too. Teachers often explain it as the same grabbing hand, pushing instead of pulling. Notice what the second truth doesn't say. It doesn't say pleasure is the cause of dukkha, or that the world is. A cup of tea isn't the problem. The thirst that won't let the cup be enough is. And that thirst is ordinary and everywhere, which is exactly why it's worth naming. Translators still differ over how to put the second and third kinds into English: becoming and non-becoming, existence and extermination, being and not-being. The sources are clear that there are three, and that all three are a kind of reaching.

segments.voice: Wait for any pull toward something pleasant, a snack, your phone, a daydream, and name it softly: pleasure. Watch for a pull toward being someone, a thought about how you look or what people think of you, and call it being; watch for any push to make something go away, an itch, a noise, a memory, and call it not-being. You don't have to act on any of them; just name the thirst, and stay.

Your line: three thirsts. Pleasure, being, not-being: each one a kind of reaching. Until tomorrow.

338.title: To be let go
338.hook: the second truth's task is to be abandoned (SN 56.11)
338.howItsDone: Buddhists in many schools practice letting go through small renunciations, such as keeping extra precepts on observance days, giving things away, and noticing cravings in meditation without following them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samudaya, the arising, and taṇhā's three thirsts, for pleasure, for being, for not-being. Your line: three thirsts.

A brahmin named Unnabha once came to the Buddha's attendant, Ananda, with what sounded like a trap. You monks, he said, live the holy life to abandon desire. But how? You'd need desire to get rid of desire. That's a circle. It's a good question, and plenty of people ask it today: if Buddhism says let go of wanting, isn't wanting to let go just more wanting? Ananda had an answer, and it involved a walk to a park.
screen: `A BRAHMIN WITH A TRAP.` → `DESIRE TO END DESIRE?` → `A WALK TO A PARK.`

segments.voice: In the first sermon, each truth has a task. Dukkha is to be understood. Its cause, craving, is pahātabba: to be abandoned, given up, let go. Not studied forever, not managed, not fed in smaller portions. Put down. That sounds harsh until you hear Ananda, in the Connected Discourses, book fifty-one. He asks the brahmin: earlier, did you have the desire to come to this park? Yes. And now that you've arrived, has that desire died down? Yes. It's the same with a monk, Ananda says. He has the desire to reach the goal, and when he reaches it, that desire falls away by itself. So not all wanting is the same. In Pali there's taṇhā, yesterday's thirst, and there's chanda, a wish to do or reach something, which can be wholesome. The path uses a good wish the way you use a boat, until the crossing's done. And letting go, in the suttas, isn't usually a single dramatic act. It's more like a hand slowly opening. You see the thirst, and what it costs. You feel it pull, and you don't follow, once, and then again, and each time it loosens a little. That's why the task is a verb that keeps going. Craving isn't an enemy to be hated; hating it would just be the third thirst again, the push to make it vanish. It's a weight you discover you don't have to carry.

Don't argue with it; on an out-breath, let the hand of the mind open a little, as if setting something down on a table. If the want comes back, that's fine: set it down again.

339.title: The third truth
339.hook: the fading away and ending of that same craving: relief is possible
339.howItsDone: Buddhists recite the third truth as part of the four noble truths, and some meditation teachers point students to brief moments when craving falls quiet as small tastes of what the third truth describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pahātabba, to be let go. A good wish can carry you there, then fall away on arrival. Your line: let it go.

You've carried the grocery bags up three flights of stairs. The handles have cut red lines into your fingers. You get the door open, swing the bags onto the counter, and there it is: a rush of lightness in your arms, so strong you almost laugh. Nothing was added. Something was put down. The Buddha used almost exactly this picture, a man setting down a heavy load, to explain the truth that turns the whole teaching from a diagnosis into good news.
screen: `THREE FLIGHTS OF STAIRS.` → `THE BAGS HIT THE COUNTER.` → `NOTHING ADDED. SOMETHING PUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: The third truth is nirodha: stopping, ending, cessation. In the first sermon the Buddha describes it as the complete fading away and ending of that very craving: giving it up, letting it go, being free of it, no longer leaning on it. Notice those words, that very craving. The third truth doesn't promise that pain will never touch your body or that loss will skip your house. It says the thirst that turns pain into suffering can end. A short sutta in the Connected Discourses, called the Burden, lays it out like the stairs. The burden is the five heaps that make up a person. The one who carries it is the person, so-and-so, of such a family. Picking the burden up is craving. Setting it down is the ending of craving. He closes with a little verse: taking up the burden is suffering in the world, and putting it down is happiness. So the relief doesn't come from getting what we want, or getting away from what we don't. It comes from the thirst itself going quiet. Some teachers point to tiny previews: the moment after an argument when the need to win drops away, the night the phone stays face down and sleep comes. What the full ending is like, the suttas mostly describe by what's absent, and that's tomorrow. Today's point is simpler. The chain isn't welded shut. It can stop.

segments.voice: For a little while, don't want the next breath to be better than this one, or the sit to end, or to go well. If a want appears, notice it, and set it down like a bag on a counter. Look for even one second where nothing is being reached for; you don't have to make it last.

Your line: it can stop. Even a second of craving letting go is a small piece of the third truth. See you tomorrow.

340.title: Blowing out
340.hook: Sariputta: nibbana is the ending of greed, hate and delusion (SN 38.1)
340.howItsDone: Buddhist schools speak of nibbana or nirvana as the goal of the path; in Theravada communities Pali verses calling it the highest happiness are often chanted, and Mahayana schools describe it in their own terms.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirodha, the third truth. Craving can fade away, like a load set down. Your line: it can stop.

A wandering ascetic named Jambukhadaka comes to Sariputta, one of the Buddha's chief monks, who, the commentary says, was his uncle. He asks the question people still ask about Buddhism. Friend Sariputta, they keep saying nibbana, nibbana. What is it? He wants it plain, not a lecture or a poem. Sariputta's answer is one sentence long, and it doesn't mention clouds or light or heaven.
screen: `AN ASCETIC MEETS SARIPUTTA.` → `WHAT IS NIBBANA?` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence, from the Connected Discourses, book thirty-eight. The destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion: that's what is called nibbana. Not a place. Not a reward handed down. The ending of three fires. The word carries the picture. Nibbana in Pali, nirvana in Sanskrit, is what happens to a flame when it goes out: blowing out, extinguishing, cooling. In the suttas, a fire burns dependent on its fuel, grass and sticks; when the fuel is used up and no more is added, it goes out. In another sutta, a wanderer named Vacchagotta asks where an awakened one goes after death. The Buddha asks him back: if a fire in front of you went out, could you say which direction it went, north, south, east or west? No, says Vacchagotta, the question doesn't apply; it went out because its fuel ran out. So nibbana isn't described as a place you travel to. And it isn't simply annihilation either; the Buddha refuses that answer too. The suttas mostly speak of it by what's absent: no greed, no hatred, no confusion. Schools of Buddhism have explored what that means in different ways, and they don't all describe it alike. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in a row of good things: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentment the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvâna the highest happiness."

segments.voice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it and watch the flame for a few breaths; if not, picture one. Then gently blow it out, watch the thin line of smoke rise and vanish, and ask where the flame went. Sit on, and let the breath be cool and quiet, like the air after the flame.

341.title: To be realized
341.hook: the third truth's task is to be tasted for oneself (SN 56.11)
341.howItsDone: Buddhists often recite the qualities of the Dhamma, including that it is to be seen here and now and invites one to come and see; teachers stress testing the teaching in one's own experience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nibbana, the blowing out of greed, hatred and delusion. Your line: the fire goes out.

Try explaining salt to someone who has never tasted it. It's white. It comes in crystals. It makes food taste more like itself. None of that is salt. Then you put a pinch on their tongue, and in half a second they know more than every sentence you said. Some things can be described, and some can only be tasted. The first sermon puts the third truth, the ending of craving, firmly in the second group, and elsewhere the Buddha uses salt to say so.
screen: `EXPLAINING SALT.` → `WHITE, CRYSTALS, SHARP.` → `A PINCH ON THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Two tasks so far: dukkha is to be understood, craving is to be let go. The third: the ending of craving is sacchikātabba, to be realized. Pali dictionaries build the word from sacchi, before your own eyes, and a verb for making. Made real for yourself, witnessed in person. Not believed on someone's say-so, not admired from a distance. The suttas have a word for the teaching that fits: ehipassiko, come and see. The Buddha doesn't ask anyone to accept the third truth because he said it. He says it can be seen. Now the salt. In the Numbered Discourses, Paharada, a lord of the titans, tells the Buddha what the titans love about the ocean. One of its wonders, he says, is that the great ocean has one taste, the taste of salt. The Buddha answers that just so, this teaching and discipline has one taste, the taste of freedom. Wherever you dip in, the generosity, the precepts, the meditation, the stories, the taste is meant to be the same. So freedom isn't only at the far end of the path, in some final moment. It's a taste, and tastes come in small amounts: a moment when resentment falls away, a morning when you're not chasing anything. Some teachers say those small tastes matter, because they show the third truth isn't just a theory. They're also clear that a pinch isn't the whole ocean.

segments.voice: Don't try to manufacture calm; look for a place where peace is already present: the stillness of your hands, the quiet between two sounds, the pause at the bottom of an out-breath. 342.title: The fourth truth
342.hook: the way that leads to the ending of dukkha: the eightfold path
342.howItsDone: Buddhists in many schools learn the noble eightfold path as the practical side of the teaching, and the eight-spoked wheel, a common Buddhist symbol, is often read as standing for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacchikātabba, to be realized, tasted for yourself like the ocean's salt. Your line: taste it.

Three truths in, look at the verbs so far. Dukkha is to be understood. Craving is to be let go. Its ending is to be realized. All three could, in principle, happen while sitting perfectly still. The fourth truth is different. It's full of ordinary verbs: speaking, acting, earning a living, making an effort, paying attention. The first three say what's true. The fourth says where to put your feet on Monday morning.
screen: `THREE TRUTHS, THREE TASKS.` → `THE ONE WITH ORDINARY VERBS.` → `WHERE TO PUT YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: The fourth truth is the way leading to the ending of dukkha. The Pali word is magga: a path, a road, a track through the forest. In the first sermon the Buddha names it: the noble eightfold path. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. The word translated right is sammā. Dictionaries also give it as properly or thoroughly, and some teachers render it complete or whole. Two things to notice. First, this path is the middle way. The sermon begins by setting aside two extremes: chasing sense pleasure, and punishing the body. The eightfold path runs between them. Second, it's not a staircase where you finish step one before starting step two. Some teachers compare it to the strands of a rope, or the spokes of a wheel, all working at once. Your speech affects your mindfulness; your mindfulness affects your view. You don't graduate from right speech. And look how ordinary much of it is: three of the eight, speech, action and livelihood, happen at the kitchen table and at work, not on a cushion. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, names the path in its list of bests: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words." Later in year two, we'll walk these eight one at a time. Today, just the map.
screen: `MAGGA: A ROAD THROUGH THE FOREST.` · `EIGHT FACTORS, NAMED.` · `STRANDS OF A ROPE, NOT STAIRS.` · `THREE AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.` · then, large: `THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Count the eight on your fingers, one per breath: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. 343.title: To be developed
343.hook: the fourth truth's task is to be walked (SN 56.11)
343.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of bhāvanā, cultivation, for meditation and for the whole path; many choose a single factor, like right speech, to work on for a day or a retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: magga, the fourth truth, eight factors working like strands of a rope. Your line: the path.

Every town has a path across a field that no one planned. No sign, no pavement. People kept walking from the bus stop to the shop until the grass gave up and a line of bare earth appeared. Nobody built it in a day, and nobody owns it. It exists because it was walked. The first sermon gives the fourth truth a task that works the same way. Not to be admired, not to be memorized: to be developed, by walking it.
screen: `A PATH NO ONE PLANNED.` → `THE GRASS GAVE UP.` → `IT EXISTS BECAUSE IT WAS WALKED.`

segments.voice: The task is bhāvetabba: to be developed, cultivated, brought into being. It comes from the verb to be, or to become, the same family as bhāvanā, one of the most common Pali words for meditation. So meditation, in this language, isn't mainly sitting still. It's bringing something into being by doing it again and again, like that path across the field. Now hold all four tasks together. Dukkha is to be understood. Craving is to be let go. Its ending is to be realized. The path is to be developed. Four truths, four verbs, and the sermon never swaps them. One way to see why: try to let go of dukkha, and you'll fight your own life. Try to understand craving forever, and you'll keep feeding it while you study it. Try to develop the ending, and you'll strain after something that comes by letting go. Each truth gets the job that fits it. Here's the week, from the top. Samudaya, the second truth: three thirsts, for pleasure, for being, for not-being. To be let go: Ananda's walk to the park, a wish that ends on arrival. Nirodha, the third truth: the burden set down. Nibbana: the fire going out, Sariputta's one-sentence answer. To be realized: the ocean with one taste. Magga, the fourth truth: eight factors like strands of a rope. And today, to be developed, the one task you can start on any Tuesday, with a single step.
screen: `BHĀVETABBA: TO BE BROUGHT INTO BEING.` · `FOUR TRUTHS, FOUR VERBS.` · `EACH TRUTH GETS ITS JOB.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `WALK IT.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the eight for today, maybe right speech, right effort or right mindfulness, and let one picture come of what it would look like in the next few hours: a kinder sentence, one task done with full attention, a pause before reacting. Hold that picture for a few breaths. Then let it go, and just sit, the way a walker rests before setting off.
Bhāvetabba. To be developed, cultivated, brought into being: the fourth truth's task, the path walked again and again until it becomes a road.
Your line: walk it. One walk at a time, the grass gives way. That's the week.
